Series::is_complex¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

bool Series::is_complex() const

What It Does¶

Returns true when the Series’ dtype is one of the two complex formats — Complex64 or Complex128 — and false for every real dtype (floating, signed and unsigned integer, and Bool).

It is a dtype test, not a value test. It reads dtype().is_complex() and nothing else: it does not scan the data for nonzero imaginary parts, and it costs nothing. A Complex64 tensor whose imaginary lane is entirely zero is still is_complex() == true — the storage layout reserves two float lanes per element regardless of what is in them.

Use it to branch before operations whose contract differs by representation rather than by content: abs() returns a magnitude for complex input and a plain absolute value for real input; sgn projects onto the unit circle for complex and returns -1/0/+1 for real; sort and the ordering comparisons reject complex entirely. Where “does this tensor carry an imaginary component at all” is the question, is_complex() answers it; where “is this particular value purely real” is the question, inspect imag instead.

is_complex() sits alongside is_floating_point and is_signed as the three category predicates on Series. Their full behavior across every scalar type:

dtype

is_complex

is_floating_point

is_signed

Bool

false

false

false

UInt8 … UInt64

false

false

false

Int8 … Int64

false

false

true

Float16, BFloat16, Float32, Float64, the 8-bit floats

false

true

true

Complex64, Complex128

true

false

true

The row that trips people up is the last one: a complex dtype is not floating-point, even though its components are floats. See is_floating_point.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

bool true for Complex64 / Complex128, false for every other dtype.

Gradient¶

Not applicable — is_complex() returns a plain bool.

Examples¶

Example 1. Across the whole scalar-type surface, only the two complex formats answer true.

for (auto st : {pluss::ScalarType::Bool, pluss::ScalarType::Int64,
                pluss::ScalarType::Float64, pluss::ScalarType::Complex64,
                pluss::ScalarType::Complex128}) {
  auto x = pluss::series::zeros({1}, st);
  std::cout << x.dtype() << " -> is_complex=" << std::boolalpha
            << x.is_complex() << "\n";
}

Output¶

bool -> is_complex=false
int64 -> is_complex=false
float64 -> is_complex=false
complex64 -> is_complex=true
complex128 -> is_complex=true

Example 2. A complex Series whose imaginary part is all zeros is still complex — the answer is about representation, not content.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(pluss::make_series({1.0f, 2.0f}),
                                pluss::make_series({0.0f, 0.0f}));
std::cout << "dtype=" << z.dtype() << " is_complex=" << std::boolalpha
          << z.is_complex() << "\n";
std::cout << "imag part: ";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.imag());

Output¶

dtype=complex64 is_complex=true
imag part: Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000]

If the real question is “is every value purely real”, test the imaginary part (z.imag().eq(0)), not is_complex().

Example 3. Pulling the real (or imaginary) part out of a complex Series gives a real floating Series — is_complex() flips to false.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(pluss::make_series({1.0f, 2.0f}),
                                pluss::make_series({3.0f, 4.0f}));
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "z.is_complex()           = " << z.is_complex() << "\n"
          << "z.real().is_complex()    = " << z.real().is_complex() << "\n"
          << "z.real().is_floating_point() = " << z.real().is_floating_point() << "\n";

Output¶

z.is_complex()           = true
z.real().is_complex()    = false
z.real().is_floating_point() = true

real and imag drop the imaginary lane and hand back a tensor in the corresponding real float dtype (Complex64 → Float32, Complex128 → Float64).

Example 4. A std::complex literal fed to make_series produces a complex Series directly.

auto z = pluss::make_series({std::complex<float>{1, 2}, {3, 4}});
std::cout << "dtype=" << z.dtype() << " is_complex=" << std::boolalpha
          << z.is_complex() << "\n";

Output¶

dtype=complex64 is_complex=true

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • is_complex() never inspects values. A complex tensor with a zero imaginary part still returns true; a real tensor holding results that “should” be complex still returns false.

  • A complex dtype is not floating-point. x.is_floating_point() || x.is_complex() is the test for “any continuous numeric data”; is_floating_point() alone silently excludes complex.

  • The ordering operations (sort, lt/gt, argsort) and reductions that depend on order reject complex input — guard with is_complex() before calling them on data of unknown dtype.

  • Converting with to is what changes the category; is_complex() only reports it.

Summary¶

is_complex() is a dtype-category predicate:

  • true only for Complex64 / Complex128

  • metadata-only — never scans for nonzero imaginary parts

  • a complex dtype is signed but not floating-point

  • pair with is_floating_point via || for an “any continuous data” check

  • Series::dtype: the exact representation, plus itemsize and the same category queries on the DType struct.

  • Series::is_floating_point / Series::is_signed: the other two category predicates.

  • Series::real / Series::imag: extract a real component (which is then no longer is_complex()).

  • pluss::series::complex: build a complex Series from real and imaginary parts.
